hints: Think about the word itself, nucleo means nucleus or positive centre, so what type of particle would be attracted to a positive centre?
Compare the two sources in the mixture, $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{NaCN}$, and decide which one can supply a negatively charged, lone pair bearing carbon species.
walkthrough:
Picture what nucleus loving means**
Think of a nucleophile as an electron rich particle hunting for a positive spot. The carbonyl carbon in ethanal, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CHO}$, is $\delta+$ because oxygen pulls electrons away. A nucleophile uses its lone pair to form a new bond to that $\delta+$ carbon.

Pick the real attacker from the mixture**
$\text{HCN}$ is a neutral molecule, but $\text{NaCN}$ fully ionises to give $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{CN}^{-}$. It is the $\text{CN}^{-}$ ion, with a lone pair on carbon, that donates its electron pair to the carbonyl carbon. So you define nucleophile as an electron pair donor and name $\text{CN}^{-}$ as the nucleophile.

Final answer: A nucleophile is a lone pair / electron pair donor.
Species acting as nucleophile: $\text{CN}^{-}$ / cyanide ion.

hints: Look at the central carbon in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$ and count how many different groups are attached to it.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral carbon**
Draw out $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$. The middle carbon is joined to four completely different groups: $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$. A carbon with four different groups is chiral, and a chiral molecule exists as non-superimposable mirror images. That type of stereoisomerism is called optical isomerism.

hints: Identify the four groups on the chiral carbon and recall how solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds show bonds coming out and going back in 3D.
Think about what makes a pair of enantiomers different, they must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed by swapping just two groups.
Remember where the asterisk goes, it marks the carbon atom with four different substituents, not the OH or CN group itself.
walkthrough:
Build the first 3D tetrahedron**
Put the chiral carbon in the centre. Attach $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{H}$ tetrahedrally. Use a normal line for two bonds in the plane, a solid wedge for a bond coming out towards you, and a hashed wedge for a bond going back away from you. This shows real 3D shape, not a flat displayed formula.

Create the mirror image partner**
Now draw its mirror image. The easiest reliable way is to copy the first structure exactly but swap the positions of any two groups, for example swap $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$ on the wedge and dash. The two structures now have the same connectivity, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$, but opposite spatial arrangement.

Label the chiral centre**
On one of the structures, place an asterisk next to the central carbon, like $\text{C}^{*}$, to show it is the chiral centre. That carbon carries four different groups, which is why the molecule is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Final answer: Draw two 3-D tetrahedral structures of $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}^{*} \text{H(OH)(CN)}$ as non-superimposable mirror images, e.g. central C with solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds to show 3D arrangement of $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CN}$.
Second structure is the mirror image of the first (two groups swapped).
Chiral centre labelled with * on the central C in one structure.

hints: Recall what happens to a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ nitrile group on heating with dilute aqueous acid, what functional group does it become?
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
A $\text{CN}$ group is hydrolysed by dilute sulfuric acid with heating to give a carboxylic acid group, $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$, plus an ammonium ion. The rest of the molecule is untouched. So $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CN}$ becomes 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H}$. The $\text{OH}$ on C2 stays exactly as it was.
